prompt: You standardise the whole dataset and then split it into train and test. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, scaling has no parameters
The mean and std were computed using test rows, so test information leaked into the preprocessing
Standardisation must be done after training the model
The test set will have mean exactly 0, which is forbidden
explanation: Any statistic learned from data (mean, std) must come from the training split only and then be applied unchanged to validation and test data.

prompt: Train values are 10, 12, 14 (mean 12, population std 1.633). What is the z-score of a test value of 30 computed with TRAIN statistics (two decimals)?
Which statement about encoding a category with 3 values (red, blue, green) is correct?
options: Label encoding 0/1/2 is always safe for linear models
One-hot encoding yields 3 columns and imposes no order between the values
One-hot encoding yields 2 columns holding the 3 values in binary
Target encoding is leak-free whatever data it is computed on
explanation: One-hot makes one binary column per category and no order. Integer codes suggest a false order; target encoding leaks if computed with the rows being predicted.

prompt: You cross a categorical feature with 100 values and another with 50 values. How many values can the crossed feature take?
explanation: $100\times50=5000$ combinations: crossing multiplies the cardinalities, which demands more data and invites overfitting.

prompt: High earners tend to leave the income field empty. This is
options: MCAR
MAR
MNAR
not a missing-value problem
explanation: The value is missing because of the value itself (missing not at random). Deleting these rows or imputing blindly loses that signal; an indicator column keeps it.

prompt: 950 negative and 50 positive examples. What is the balanced class weight of the positive class $N/(2n_c)$?
You oversample the minority class. When and where must this be done?
options: On the whole dataset before splitting, so the split is balanced
On the test set as well, for fairness
On the training split only, after splitting; evaluate on data with the real class ratio
Never, it always breaks the model
explanation: Oversampling creates duplicates (or synthetic points). Done before the split, copies end up on both sides and inflate the score; evaluating on resampled data measures a distribution that does not exist in production.

prompt: A model trained on a 50/50 resampled set outputs 0.8 for a case. The real positive rate is 1%. What is the corrected probability (three decimals)?
explanation: Multiply by $\pi_{true}/\pi_{bal}$ per class and renormalise: $0.8\cdot0.02=0.016$ versus $0.2\cdot1.98=0.396$; $0.016/0.412=0.039$.

prompt: Pure-noise labels, 500 noise features. You pick the 10 features most correlated with the label using ALL rows and then cross-validate. The score is far above 50%. The best explanation is
options: The model found real structure
Feature selection used the labels of the evaluation rows (leakage); selection must be repeated inside each training split
Cross-validation is invalid for noise
Nearest-mean classifiers are too powerful
explanation: With many candidate features some always correlate with a small sample by chance. Selecting them with the test rows included builds the test labels into the model.

prompt: You predict daily sales. Which split avoids leakage?
options: Random 80/20 split of all days
Train on earlier weeks, validate and test on later weeks
Train on the last weeks, test on the earliest
Shuffle rows, then take every fifth day as test
explanation: Time-correlated data must be split by time so that the model never sees information from the future of the period it is evaluated on.
